name: Taj Mahal
builder: Mughal emperor Shah Jahan
summary: The white-marble mausoleum Shah Jahan built for Mumtaz Mahal is the crowning jewel of Mughal architecture and India's most visited monument. Its perfect symmetry, pietra dura inlay and riverside charbagh gardens draw millions each year at sunrise and moonlight viewings.

name: Agra Fort
builder: Mughal emperor Akbar (extended by Shah Jahan)
summary: Akbar's massive red-sandstone citadel on the Yamuna served as the Mughal seat of power before Delhi. Inside are Shah Jahan's marble palaces, including the Musamman Burj where he was imprisoned within sight of the Taj Mahal.

name: Fatehpur Sikri
builder: Mughal emperor Akbar
summary: Akbar's short-lived red-sandstone capital, built to honour the Sufi saint Salim Chishti, was abandoned within decades, leaving a perfectly preserved Mughal ghost city. Highlights include the towering Buland Darwaza, the Panch Mahal and the saint's marble dargah.

name: Churches and Convents of Goa (Basilica of Bom Jesus, Old Goa)
builder: Portuguese colonial administration and religious orders
summary: Old Goa's baroque and Manueline churches, led by the Basilica of Bom Jesus holding the relics of St Francis Xavier, spread Renaissance church art across Asia. The Se Cathedral and Church of St Francis of Assisi complete one of Asia's grandest Christian ensembles.

name: Hampi (Vijayanagara)
builder: Vijayanagara Empire (Sangama to Tuluva dynasties)
summary: The boulder-strewn ruins of Vijayanagara, once among the world's richest cities, sprawl along the Tungabhadra with royal enclosures, elephant stables, stepped tanks and the iconic stone chariot. Sacked in 1565, the vast site is now a magnet for travellers and climbers alike.

name: Buddhist Monuments at Sanchi
builder: Emperor Ashoka (Maurya), enlarged under Shunga and Satavahana rule
summary: Sanchi's Great Stupa, begun by Ashoka in the 3rd century BCE, is the oldest stone structure in India, ringed by exquisitely carved toranas depicting the Buddha's life. The hilltop complex traces 1,400 years of Buddhist art in one serene setting.

name: Humayun's Tomb
builder: Empress Bega Begum for Mughal emperor Humayun; architect Mirak Mirza Ghiyas
summary: The first great garden tomb of the subcontinent, Humayun's red-sandstone and marble mausoleum pioneered the charbagh layout later perfected at the Taj Mahal. Beautifully restored, it anchors a necropolis of over 100 Mughal-era tombs near the Nizamuddin dargah.

name: Qutb Minar and its Monuments
builder: Qutb-ud-din Aibak and Iltutmish (Delhi Sultanate)
summary: The 72.5-metre fluted Qutb Minar, begun in 1192, towers over Delhi's earliest mosque, the Quwwat-ul-Islam, and the rust-free 4th-century Iron Pillar. The complex marks the dawn of Indo-Islamic architecture in India.

name: Darjeeling Himalayan Railway (Mountain Railways of India)
builder: British colonial government / Gillanders Arbuthnot & Co.
protection: Indian Railways; UNESCO World Heritage (inscribed 1999, extended 2005 and 2008)
summary: The 'Toy Train' has climbed from the plains to Darjeeling at 2,200 m since 1881 through loops and zig-zags, including the famous Batasia Loop. Steam-hauled joyrides past tea gardens make it the most beloved of India's three World Heritage mountain railways.

name: Chhatrapati Shivaji Terminus
builder: British Raj; architect F.W. Stevens
protection: Indian Railways heritage; UNESCO World Heritage (inscribed 2004)
summary: Mumbai's flamboyant Victorian Gothic railway station, completed in 1887 as Victoria Terminus, fuses Gothic Revival with Indian ornament in a riot of turrets, gargoyles and stained glass. It remains one of the busiest working railway stations in the world.

name: Champaner-Pavagadh Archaeological Park
builder: Sultan Mahmud Begada of Gujarat (earlier hill settlements from 8th century)
summary: The only complete, unaltered pre-Mughal Islamic city in India, Champaner was Sultan Mahmud Begada's capital before being abandoned after 1536. Its Jami Masjid blends Hindu and Islamic craftsmanship beneath the sacred Pavagadh hill.

name: Red Fort Complex
builder: Mughal emperor Shah Jahan
summary: Shah Jahan's red-sandstone palace-fortress of Shahjahanabad held the Peacock Throne and remains India's most symbolic monument, where the Prime Minister hoists the flag every Independence Day. Its Diwan-i-Khas and marble pavilions epitomise late Mughal splendour.

name: Jantar Mantar, Jaipur
builder: Maharaja Sawai Jai Singh II
protection: Rajasthan State Archaeology; UNESCO World Heritage (inscribed 2010)
summary: The best preserved of Jai Singh II's five stone observatories, Jaipur's Jantar Mantar includes the Samrat Yantra, the world's largest sundial, accurate to two seconds. Its monumental instruments still track the heavens with naked-eye precision.

name: Chittorgarh Fort (Hill Forts of Rajasthan)
builder: Mori dynasty; expanded by Sisodia Rajputs of Mewar
summary: India's largest fort spreads over a 180-m-high plateau, scarred by three epic sieges and jauhars that made it the ultimate symbol of Rajput honour. Vijay Stambha (Tower of Victory), Rana Kumbha's palace and Padmini's water pavilion crown its 13-km ramparts.

name: Kumbhalgarh Fort (Hill Forts of Rajasthan)
builder: Rana Kumbha of Mewar; architect Mandan
summary: Kumbhalgarh's 36-km wall, often called the second longest in the world after the Great Wall of China, snakes over the Aravalli hills guarding Mewar's second capital. It is the birthplace of Maharana Pratap and glows spectacularly during evening light shows.

name: Amber Fort (Hill Forts of Rajasthan)
builder: Raja Man Singh I of the Kachwaha dynasty
protection: Rajasthan State Archaeology; UNESCO World Heritage (inscribed 2013)
summary: The honey-coloured palace-fort of the Kachwaha rajas rises above Maota Lake outside Jaipur, its Sheesh Mahal (Mirror Palace) glittering with thousands of mirrored mosaics. Ramparts link it to Jaigarh Fort, home of the world's largest wheeled cannon.

name: Jaisalmer Fort (Hill Forts of Rajasthan)
builder: Rawal Jaisal, Bhati Rajput dynasty
summary: The golden-sandstone Sonar Qila rising from the Thar Desert is one of the world's few living forts, with thousands still residing in its lanes of havelis, temples and rooftop cafes. At sunset the whole citadel glows like a sandcastle from a fairy tale.

name: Rani-ki-Vav (Queen's Stepwell), Patan
builder: Queen Udayamati of the Chaulukya (Solanki) dynasty
summary: Built as an inverted temple to water, this seven-storey stepwell holds over 500 principal sculptures of Vishnu's avatars and celestial maidens. Buried by Saraswati river silt for centuries, its pristine carvings now feature on India's 100-rupee note.

name: Nalanda Mahavihara
builder: Kumaragupta I (Gupta dynasty), patronised by Harsha and the Palas
summary: The world's first great residential university taught Buddhist philosophy, logic and medicine to some 10,000 monks, drawing scholars like Xuanzang from across Asia. Its red-brick monasteries, stupas and shrines flourished for 800 years before destruction around 1200 CE.

name: Capitol Complex, Chandigarh (Le Corbusier)
builder: Le Corbusier for the Government of Punjab / Government of India
protection: Chandigarh Administration; UNESCO World Heritage (inscribed 2016, transnational Le Corbusier serial site)
summary: Le Corbusier's monumental concrete ensemble of the High Court, Secretariat, Legislative Assembly and Open Hand Monument crowns independent India's first planned city. It is India's only modernist World Heritage architecture, visitable on guided tours.

name: Khangchendzonga National Park
builder: Sacred landscape of the Lepcha and Bhutia peoples; park notified 1977
protection: Sikkim Forest Department; UNESCO World Heritage (mixed site, inscribed 2016)
summary: India's only mixed World Heritage site pairs the world's third-highest peak with a living sacred landscape of caves, lakes and monasteries central to Sikkimese Buddhist and Lepcha belief. Trekkers on the Goecha La trail walk beneath Khangchendzonga's guardian summit.

name: Historic City of Ahmadabad
builder: Sultan Ahmad Shah I of Gujarat
protection: Ahmedabad Municipal Corporation / ASI monuments; UNESCO World Heritage (inscribed 2017)
summary: India's first World Heritage City preserves 600 years of walled-city life: carved wooden havelis in tight-knit pols, the Bhadra citadel, Sidi Saiyyed's famed jali screens and Jama Masjid. Heritage walks at dawn reveal a living medieval trading town.

name: Victorian Gothic and Art Deco Ensembles of Mumbai
builder: British Raj architects and Indian mercantile patrons
protection: Municipal heritage regulations; UNESCO World Heritage (inscribed 2018)
summary: Facing each other across the Oval Maidan stand two waves of Mumbai's ambition: 19th-century Victorian Gothic public buildings like the High Court and university, and the world's second-largest collection of Art Deco apartments and cinemas along Marine Drive.

name: Jaipur City (Walled City)
builder: Maharaja Sawai Jai Singh II; architect Vidyadhar Bhattacharya
protection: State/Municipal heritage administration; UNESCO World Heritage (inscribed 2019)
summary: The Pink City's 1727 grid plan, based on Vedic principles, packs in the Hawa Mahal's honeycomb facade, City Palace, bazaars and Jantar Mantar behind rose-coloured ramparts. It is one of South Asia's earliest and finest planned cities.

name: Dholavira: A Harappan City
builder: Harappan (Indus Valley) Civilisation
summary: On an island in the white salt desert of the Rann of Kutch lie the remains of a 5,000-year-old Harappan metropolis famed for its sophisticated stone architecture and cascading water reservoirs. Its ancient signboard bears the world's oldest known large inscription.

name: Santiniketan
builder: Debendranath Tagore and Rabindranath Tagore
protection: Visva-Bharati University / Ministry of Education; UNESCO World Heritage (inscribed 2023)
summary: Rabindranath Tagore transformed his father's ashram into an open-air university where classes meet under mango trees and art, music and internationalism flourish. Murals, sculptures and the poet's homes make it a pilgrimage for lovers of Bengal's cultural renaissance.

name: Moidams – the Mound-Burial System of the Ahom Dynasty, Charaideo
builder: Ahom dynasty (Tai-Ahom kings)
summary: Grassy pyramid-like burial mounds of Ahom royalty dot the sacred hillocks of Charaideo, the dynasty's first capital, often called the 'Pyramids of Assam'. Inscribed in 2024, they are Northeast India's first cultural World Heritage site.

name: Raigad Fort (Maratha Military Landscapes of India)
builder: Chhatrapati Shivaji Maharaj (rebuilt from earlier Rairi fort)
summary: Shivaji's mountaintop capital, where he was crowned Chhatrapati in 1674, commands the Sahyadris from 820 metres, reached today by ropeway or 1,700 steps. Its royal court, market street and the king's samadhi crown the flagship of the 12-fort Maratha Military Landscapes.

name: Gingee Fort (Maratha Military Landscapes of India)
builder: Kon dynasty origins; expanded by Vijayanagara Nayaks, held by Marathas under Rajaram
summary: Called the 'Troy of the East' by the French, Gingee's triple-hill citadel of Rajagiri, Krishnagiri and Chandrayandurg withstood a seven-year Mughal siege sheltering Chhatrapati Rajaram. It is the sole Tamil Nadu component of the Maratha Military Landscapes.

name: Sindhudurg Fort (Maratha Military Landscapes of India)
builder: Chhatrapati Shivaji Maharaj
summary: Built by Shivaji on a rocky island off Malvan with foundations of molten lead, Sindhudurg anchored the pioneering Maratha navy. Boats ferry visitors across turquoise waters to ramparts hiding a rare temple to Shivaji himself.

name: Ancient Buddhist Site of Sarnath
builder: Emperor Ashoka (Maurya); expanded through Kushan and Gupta periods
summary: Where the Buddha preached his first sermon around 528 BCE, Ashoka raised stupas and the lion-capital pillar that became India's national emblem. The Dhamek Stupa and monastery ruins near Varanasi became India's 45th World Heritage site in July 2026.

name: Golconda Fort
builder: Qutb Shahi dynasty (on earlier Kakatiya and Bahmani fort)
summary: The granite citadel of the Qutb Shahis guarded the diamond markets that produced the Koh-i-Noor and Hope diamonds. Its legendary acoustics let a clap at the gate be heard at the hilltop durbar hall nearly a kilometre away.

name: Charminar
builder: Sultan Muhammad Quli Qutb Shah
summary: Hyderabad's four-minareted signature monument was raised in 1591 to mark the founding of the new Qutb Shahi capital. Around it swirl the Laad Bazaar's bangle shops and the aromas of the old city's famous street food.

name: Gwalior Fort
builder: Legendary founding by Suraj Sen; Man Mandir Palace by Man Singh Tomar (1486-1516)
summary: Babur reputedly called this sandstone giant 'the pearl amongst fortresses in India'. Its blue-tiled Man Mandir Palace, colossal rock-cut Jain tirthankaras and one of the world's oldest inscriptions of zero make Gwalior a layered thousand-year epic.

name: Mehrangarh Fort
builder: Rao Jodha, Rathore dynasty of Marwar
summary: Rising 120 metres sheer above Jodhpur's blue houses, Mehrangarh is among India's most dramatic forts, its palaces filled with palanquins, howdahs and miniature paintings in a superbly curated museum. Ziplines and evening concerts add modern thrills to Rathore grandeur.

name: Adalaj Stepwell (Adalaj ni Vav)
builder: Queen Rudabai; completed under Sultan Mahmud Begada
summary: Five storeys of intricately carved sandstone descend to cool water in this 1498 stepwell near Ahmedabad, its octagonal shaft blending Solanki and Islamic ornament. Legend ties its beauty to Queen Rudabai's tragic bargain with the sultan who completed it.

name: Bidar Fort
builder: Sultan Ahmad Shah Wali Bahmani
summary: When the Bahmani sultans shifted their capital to Bidar in 1427 they rebuilt this vast fort with Persian-style palaces, the tile-clad Rangin Mahal and a triple moat cut from red laterite. Nearby stand the Bahmani tombs and the medieval Madrasa of Mahmud Gawan.

name: Gol Gumbaz
builder: Mohammed Adil Shah of Bijapur; architect Yaqut of Dabul
summary: The mausoleum of Mohammed Adil Shah in Vijayapura carries one of the world's largest domes, spanning some 44 metres unsupported. Its whispering gallery repeats the faintest sound seven times around the vast chamber.

name: Vikramashila Mahavihara
builder: King Dharmapala of the Pala dynasty
summary: Founded by Dharmapala around 800 CE as a rival to Nalanda, Vikramashila trained masters of tantric Buddhism including Atisha, who carried its teachings to Tibet. Excavations at Antichak reveal a huge cruciform stupa ringed by 208 monastic cells.

name: Amaravati Mahastupa
builder: Begun under Maurya-era patronage; embellished by the Satavahana and Ikshvaku dynasties
summary: Once among the grandest stupas in the Buddhist world, Amaravati's Mahachaitya was sheathed in limestone reliefs whose 'Amaravati school' shaped Buddhist art across Asia. The serene site and its museum sit beside the Krishna river near the new Andhra capital named for it.

name: Nagarjunakonda
builder: Ikshvaku dynasty (capital Vijayapuri)
summary: The great Buddhist city of the Ikshvakus, with its stupas, monasteries and amphitheatre, was moved block by block to an island museum when the Nagarjuna Sagar dam flooded the valley in 1960. A scenic boat ride now delivers visitors to relics of 3rd-century Andhra.

name: Warangal Fort
builder: Kakatiya rulers Ganapati Deva and Rudrama Devi
summary: Four freestanding Kakatiya Kala Thoranam gateways — now Telangana's state emblem — mark the heart of the 13th-century Kakatiya capital, ringed by earthen and stone walls. The ruined Swayambhu complex scatters exquisite black-basalt sculpture across lawns.

name: Daulatabad (Devagiri) Fort
builder: Yadava king Bhillama V; expanded by Delhi Sultans and Ahmadnagar rulers
summary: The conical hill-fort of Devagiri, briefly Muhammad bin Tughluq's infamous replacement capital for Delhi, is defended by moats, spiralling dark passages and sheer scarps that made it nearly impregnable. The Chand Minar victory tower rises 30 metres within.

name: Shaniwar Wada
builder: Peshwa Baji Rao I
summary: The fortified palace of the Peshwas ruled much of India in the 18th century until an 1828 fire gutted its teak mansions, leaving mighty gates and garden foundations. An evening sound-and-light show retells Pune's Maratha glory and the palace's ghostly legends.

name: Victoria Memorial
builder: British Raj; architect William Emerson
protection: Victoria Memorial Hall Trust, Ministry of Culture
summary: Kolkata's white-marble tribute to Queen Victoria, completed in 1921, blends British and Mughal design beneath a rotating Angel of Victory. Its galleries hold a superb collection of Raj-era paintings, manuscripts and Calcutta history.

name: Gateway of India
builder: British Raj; architect George Wittet
summary: Built to commemorate King George V's 1911 visit, the basalt Indo-Saracenic arch on Mumbai's harbour witnessed the last British troops leave India in 1948. It remains the city's favourite waterfront promenade and the jetty for Elephanta ferries.

name: The Residency, Lucknow
builder: Nawabs Asaf-ud-Daula and Saadat Ali Khan for the British Resident
summary: The shattered, cannonball-pocked ruins of the British Residency stand frozen since the 147-day Siege of Lucknow in 1857, one of the defining episodes of India's First War of Independence. Lawns, a cemetery and a museum make it a hauntingly peaceful memorial.

name: Cellular Jail (Kala Pani)
builder: British colonial government
protection: National Memorial, Andaman and Nicobar Administration
summary: The dreaded 'Kala Pani' penal colony at Port Blair held freedom fighters like Veer Savarkar in 698 solitary cells radiating from a central tower. Now a National Memorial, its nightly sound-and-light show narrates the prisoners' sacrifice.

name: Mandu (Jahaz Mahal and Royal Enclave)
builder: Malwa Sultans Dilawar Khan, Hoshang Shah and Ghiyas-ud-din Khalji
summary: Perched on a monsoon-swept plateau, the deserted Malwa capital charms with the 'ship palace' Jahaz Mahal floating between two lakes, Hoshang Shah's marble tomb (said to have inspired the Taj) and the romance of Baz Bahadur and Rani Roopmati. It is one of India's great Afghan-architecture ensembles.

name: Orchha (Jehangir Mahal and Fort Complex)
builder: Bundela Rajputs; Jehangir Mahal by Raja Bir Singh Deo (c. 1610)
summary: On an island in the Betwa river, Orchha's Bundela palaces mix Rajput and Mughal styles, crowned by the domed Jehangir Mahal built for a single imperial visit. Riverside chhatris (royal cenotaphs) at sunset are among central India's loveliest sights.

name: Tomb of Sher Shah Suri, Sasaram
builder: Sher Shah Suri; architect Mir Muhammad Aliwal Khan
summary: The red-sandstone mausoleum of the Afghan emperor who built the Grand Trunk Road rises from the middle of a lake at Sasaram, a masterpiece of Indo-Afghan architecture sometimes called the 'second Taj Mahal'. Its 37-metre dome was among the largest in India when finished in 1545.

name: Fort St. George, Chennai
builder: British East India Company
summary: The first English fortress in India (1644) seeded the city of Madras and today houses the Tamil Nadu legislature, a fine colonial museum and St Mary's Church, the oldest Anglican church east of Suez. Clive of India and Elihu Yale both served within its walls.

name: Mattancherry Palace (Dutch Palace), Kochi
builder: Portuguese (gifted to the Raja of Cochin); renovated by the Dutch in 1663
summary: Gifted by the Portuguese to the Cochin royal family and later refurbished by the Dutch, this quadrangular palace shelters some of India's finest Kerala murals depicting the Ramayana in glowing ochres. It sits amid Kochi's spice markets and the historic Jew Town synagogue quarter.

name: Kangra Fort
builder: Katoch dynasty of Trigarta (ancient origins; recorded from early first millennium)
summary: Claimed as one of the oldest forts in India, the Katoch stronghold at the confluence of the Banganga and Manjhi rivers was coveted by Mahmud of Ghazni, Jahangir and Ranjit Singh alike. Earthquake-scarred ramparts and temple courtyards overlook the Dhauladhar range.

name: Leh Palace
builder: King Sengge Namgyal of Ladakh
summary: The nine-storey mud-brick palace of the Namgyal kings looms over Leh's old town like a miniature Potala, abandoned when Dogra forces invaded in the 1830s. Restored by the ASI, its rooftop offers sweeping views of the Indus valley and Stok Kangri.

name: Kangla Fort, Imphal
builder: Meitei kings of Manipur (traditional founding by Nongda Lairen Pakhangba, 33 CE)
protection: Kangla Fort Board, Government of Manipur
summary: The sacred seat of Manipur's Meitei kings for nearly two millennia, Kangla on the Imphal river blends citadel, coronation site and shrine, guarded by the rebuilt Kangla-Sha dragon-lions. It remained the royal capital until the Anglo-Manipur War of 1891.

name: Rang Ghar, Sivasagar
builder: Ahom king Pramatta Singha
summary: Asia's oldest surviving amphitheatre, the two-storey oval Rang Ghar hosted Ahom royalty watching buffalo fights and games during Rongali Bihu. Its boat-shaped roof and rice-and-egg mortar masonry showcase Ahom engineering near the great Sivasagar tank.

name: Ratnagiri Monastery (Odisha Diamond Triangle)
builder: Gupta-era foundation, flourishing under the Bhaumakara dynasty
summary: Crowning a hill above the Birupa river, Ratnagiri was a great Mahayana and Vajrayana monastic university whose exquisitely carved doorway and colossal Buddha heads rival Nalanda. With nearby Udayagiri and Lalitgiri it forms Odisha's Buddhist 'Diamond Triangle'.

name: Hazarduari Palace, Murshidabad
builder: Nawab Nazim Humayun Jah; architect Duncan Macleod
summary: The 'palace of a thousand doors' on the Bhagirathi river recalls Murshidabad's days as Bengal's capital before Plassey, its Italianate halls now an ASI museum of armoury, chandeliers and Nawabi treasures. Some of its 1,000 doors are false, built to confuse intruders.
